Systematic downward drift in the measured quantity itself, decoupled from instrument-to-instrument agreement
Instruments measure genuinely different observables; pendulum and resonator systems are decoupled despite nominal co-location
All instruments are affected by a common slow environmental drift, but measurement noise is large enough to mask instrument-to-instrument synchrony on short timescales

pendulum_obs has drifted out of calibration or experienced a mechanical change (damping loss, pivot wear, amplitude decay) between day 10 and day 27, producing a real downward shift in observed beat frequency independent of environmental causes.

Observatory location (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) experiences larger environmental fluctuations than lab location (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab)—e.g., greater temperature swing, humidity variation, or vibration—producing coherent but location-dependent drift: lab instruments drift slowly, observatory instruments drift faster.

True physical signal (common environmental driver affecting all instruments) is small and aperiodic; measurement noise is large; drift appears as a statistical artifact of baseline overfitting—baseline period (n=70–144 per instrument) happened to sample a high region of noise, post-baseline period samples lower region, producing false downward drift signal.

Baseline period (days 1–10) included calibration and instrument warm-up; instruments were not in thermal/mechanical equilibrium. Post-baseline period (days 11–20) reflects approach to equilibrium, producing downward drift as instruments relax toward true operating state. This is especially pronounced in observatory instruments, which are more exposed to environmental transients.

Data recording or archival error: post-baseline data (days 11–20) were systematically recorded at a lower calibration setting, different sensor gain, or with a processing artifact (e.g., all post-baseline values divided by a common factor ~1.002 or offset downward by a constant bias).

pendulum_obs and resonator_obs share a common uncontrolled systematic bias (e.g., both affected by a 3-day-lagged environmental driver, or both driven by an identical post-processing artifact), producing spurious perfect correlation that masks independent physical measurement.

The r=1.000 correlation is a statistical artifact of small sample size or cherry-picked lag search: with n=110 and many lags tested, random noise can occasionally align perfectly by chance, especially if one or both time series are correlated with themselves at multiple lags (inflating false-positive likelihood in permutation search).

pendulum_obs data were mislabeled or misaligned in time during archival: trial numbering or timestamps were offset by 3 days relative to resonator_obs, causing two different instruments' readings to be cross-matched at offset lags. The r=1.000 reflects alignment of correct data with incorrect index, not a physical correlation.

The drift pattern (all four instruments drifting downward) is genuine environmental change (temperature decrease, humidity increase, barometric shift) affecting all instruments similarly, with location-dependent magnitude due to differential shielding; the perfect r=1.000 correlation is a separate coincidental artifact or data error, not a signal of common driver.

Residual: an unidentified systematic error in my correlation analysis, data labeling, or instrument configuration that I have not yet recognized; alternatively, a genuine but exotic physical mechanism (coupled oscillation between pendulum and resonator, mechanical resonance at 3-day period driven by unidentified source) that demands investigation rather than dismissal.

Data labeling or file-handling error: pendulum_obs trials are misaligned in time or mislabeled relative to resonator_obs, causing cross-correlation at offset lag to match data that are actually from the same calendar period

Common environmental driver with 3-day lag structure (e.g., thermal mass of building envelope, humidity diffusion delay) affecting pendulum_obs and resonator_obs identically, producing spurious perfect correlation that masks independent sensor physics

Data processing or logging pipeline artifact: resonator_obs values are numerically derived from or contaminated by pendulum_obs values (e.g., common data logger, shared post-processing step, accidental copy-paste, or feedback between instruments in analysis code), making one a deterministic function of the other

Genuine but unrecognized systematic error in my correlation-analysis method (e.g., code bug, incorrect lag-search procedure, misapplied statistical test) that produced spurious r=1.000 for this one instrument pair

Genuine physical coupling between pendulum and resonator (e.g., pendulum vibrations mechanically drive resonator frequency via shared mounting or structure) that happens to exhibit a 3-day-lagged feedback or resonance pattern, producing perfect correlation
